title: Quantum Computing's Real Threat To Product Supply Chains
excerpt: Imagine a refrigerated container crossing the Atlantic sometime in the 2030s. Inside are cell therapies. Each one is made from a single patient's own cells and cannot be replaced. The container reports a steady temperature of 4 degrees, and the data loggers agree. Every reading is digitally signed. Every firmware update is authenticated. The electronic bill of lading that releases the cargo at the port has a valid signature. All of it is fake. The firmware was changed weeks earlier, and the update was signed with a key forged by a quantum computer. The product spoiled mid-ocean. Nobody finds out until patients do not respond to treatment.This is hypothetical, but it is not far-fetched. It also shows what most boardroom discussions about quantum computing miss. For companies that make, move or store physical goods, the biggest quantum risk is not that someone reads their data. It is that someone can forge the signatures that control their physical assets.The Supply Chain Runs On CryptographyTake a global biopharmaceutical company that makes biologics in Ireland and ships them to US hospitals. Its products pass through fill-finish lines, smart insulated shippers, refrigerated containers, air freighters, trucks and distribution centres.Each of those handovers now depends on public key cryptography. Serialisation data moves between trading partners under the US Drug Supply Chain Security Act (DSCSA) and Europe's Falsified Medicines Directive. Internet of Things (IoT) loggers report temperature and location over cellular networks. Container controllers accept remote firmware updates and temperature commands. Equipment vendors maintain remote maintenance connections into the plant. Electronic bills of lading transfer ownership of cargo through digital signatures. Chain-of-identity records tie each cell and gene therapy vial to one patient. Almost all of this rests on two encryption methods, Rivest-Shamir-Adleman (RSA) and elliptic curve cryptography (ECC). A large enough quantum computer would break both.'Harvest Now, Decrypt Later' Is Only Half The ProblemExecutives who follow quantum risk usually know the 'harvest now, decrypt later' threat. Adversaries steal or intercept encrypted data today and store it until future quantum computers can decrypt it. The theft is getting faster. Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 found that the fastest quarter of intrusions reached data exfiltration in 72 minutes in 2025, compared with 285 minutes in 2024. Supply chain data stays valuable for a long time. That includes supplier pricing, bills of materials and patient-linked logistics records. It also includes clinical trial shipment patterns, which show where trials run and how fast they are enrolling. A rival who decrypts five-year-old trial supply data in 2032 still learns something useful. But confidentiality is the half of the problem people already know. Integrity is the more dangerous half. Once signatures can be forged, an attacker does not just read your supply chain. They can give it orders.How Forged Signatures Cause Physical HarmForged firmware: Containers and loggers accept signed updates. If the signature can be forged, an attacker can change temperature settings or make devices report 'in range' while the product spoils. That is sabotage at scale, with no broken seal to find.Forged ownership and release documents: A forged bill of lading or release message can send a high-value shipment to the wrong truck. Cargo theft no longer needs an insider.Forged partner identities: If an attacker can impersonate a trading partner in the drug tracing system, they can slip counterfeit or diverted products into legitimate channels. For cell therapies, an altered chain-of-identity record is a patient safety disaster, not just a compliance failure.A fourth problem moves more slowly. Pharmaceutical batch, serialization and chain-of-identity records are kept for years and may be used in lawsuits for decades. Once old-style signatures can be forged, anyone can question whether a record signed that way is authentic.The Signature GapThere is a trap here. The industry is adopting quantum-safe encryption faster than quantum-safe signatures. Analysts reviewing the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) January 2026 guidance on post-quantum products pointed to a 'signature gap'. Many products support the National Institute of Standards and Technology's (NIST) new standard for exchanging encryption keys (ML-KEM), but support for its signature standard (ML-DSA) is far less common. The result is a 'half-migrated' reality where data in transit is protected against 'harvest now, decrypt later' attacks, but the systems are still vulnerable to future quantum impersonation.For a bank, that gap is serious. In a supply chain, where signatures control physical equipment, it is the main risk. Replacing signatures means changing the root keys everything else trusts, along with the security hardware that stores them, across dozens of organisations. That is much harder than switching on a new encryption setting.Why This Is A 2026 DecisionExecutives often ask when a quantum computer able to break today's encryption will arrive. Estimates vary. One 2026 analysis says RSA-breaking machines could arrive by 2030, plus or minus three years, and Forrester argues that practical quantum computing by 2030 is likely. For supply chains, though, that is the wrong question.The better question is how long the equipment you buy this year will stay in service. Refrigerated containers run for over a decade, and industrial controllers often last 20 years or more. A logger shipped today with a fixed RSA key that cannot be updated in the field may still be working when quantum attacks become practical.Researchers frame this with a simple test called Mosca's inequality. Add two numbers: how long your data must stay secret, or your equipment must stay trustworthy, and how long it will take you to migrate.If the total is longer than the time until a quantum attack is possible, you are already exposed. In supply chains, equipment lifespan is often what pushes companies over the line. That means purchasing decisions made in 2026 will set quantum exposure in the 2030s.Policymakers have noticed. In June 2026, the White House issued Executive Order 14409, which warns that "the advent of large-scale quantum computers, particularly in the hands of adversaries, will pose a significant threat to widely used cryptographic security systems." Federal purchasing standards usually spread to private suppliers. Pharma, defence and logistics firms that sell to the government will feel the effect first.Why The Business Risk Is Easy To UnderestimateFrom a risk management view, quantum risk has three features that most corporate risk frameworks handle poorly. It hits everyone at once. A broken algorithm does not affect one company. It affects every company that uses it, at the same moment. For cyber insurers, that looks more like a natural catastrophe than a series of separate claims, and the market has struggled to price that kind of system-wide exposure.It may fall between insurance policies. If forged firmware spoils a shipment, is that a cyber loss, a marine cargo loss or a product recall loss? Each policy may exclude it. The first quantum attackers will probably be nation states, so exclusions for war and state-backed attacks add more uncertainty.The costs come first and the losses come later. Companies pay to fix the problem now, but the damage arrives years from now, and quarterly incentives favour waiting. Smaller carriers and logistics providers are the weakest links in any multi-company chain, and they have the least money and motivation to upgrade. Their inaction exposes everyone else.What Leaders Should Do Now1. Map your cryptography, including your partners'. Build a full inventory of where your company uses encryption and signatures, sometimes called a cryptographic bill of materials. Cover enterprise resource planning (ERP) and warehouse systems, partner connections, IoT devices and controllers, and the hardware that stores your keys. Require key suppliers to provide the same.2. Rank by impact, not by system. Upgrade first the assets whose compromise would cause physical harm or that will stay in service the longest. Firmware signing for cold-chain devices and remote access to manufacturing usually top the list.3. Block data harvesting now. Hybrid encryption combines today's methods with quantum-safe ones, and it is already available in mainstream web security and virtual private network (VPN) software. Turn it on for partner data exchanges and vendor maintenance links.4. Make signatures the priority, and buy flexibility. Every new device contract should require two things: quantum-safe firmware signing and the ability to change keys and algorithms later without replacing hardware, often called crypto agility.The goal is long-term flexibility rather than performing a one-time upgrade. Small battery-powered loggers may be too limited for large quantum-safe signatures. For those, have the logger use lightweight encryption to talk to a nearby gateway, and let the gateway handle the quantum-safe security.5. Coordinate with partners and check your insurance. No company can upgrade a supply chain alone. Push for shared timelines through industry bodies such as GS1, the Digital Container Shipping Association and the International Air Transport Association (IATA). Write quantum readiness milestones into supplier contracts, with cost-sharing for smaller partners. Ask your broker directly which policy pays if a forged signature spoils a shipment.Quantum computing usually reaches the boardroom as an IT upgrade. For any company that makes, moves or stores physical goods, it is really a question of operational resilience. The same cryptography that protects your data also controls your containers, releases your cargo and proves your products are genuine.The companies that get through the quantum transition well will not be the ones that guessed the date right. They will be the ones that stopped buying equipment that cannot survive it.
content:
Imagine a refrigerated container crossing the Atlantic sometime in the 2030s. Inside are cell therapies. Each one is made from a single patient's own cells and cannot be replaced. The container reports a steady temperature of 4 degrees, and the data loggers agree. Every reading is digitally signed. 

Every firmware update is authenticated. The electronic bill of lading that releases the cargo at the port has a valid signature. All of it is fake. The firmware was changed weeks earlier, and the update was signed with a key forged by a quantum computer. The product spoiled mid-ocean. Nobody finds out until patients do not respond to treatment.

This is hypothetical, but it is not far-fetched. It also shows what most boardroom discussions about quantum computing miss. For companies that make, move or store physical goods, the biggest quantum risk is not that someone reads their data. It is that someone can forge the signatures that control their physical assets.

The Supply Chain Runs On Cryptography
Take a global biopharmaceutical company that makes biologics in Ireland and ships them to US hospitals. Its products pass through fill-finish lines, smart insulated shippers, refrigerated containers, air freighters, trucks and distribution centres.

Each of those handovers now depends on public key cryptography. Serialisation data moves between trading partners under the US Drug Supply Chain Security Act (DSCSA) and Europe's Falsified Medicines Directive. Internet of Things (IoT) loggers report temperature and location over cellular networks. Container controllers accept remote firmware updates and temperature commands. Equipment vendors maintain remote maintenance connections into the plant. 

Electronic bills of lading transfer ownership of cargo through digital signatures. Chain-of-identity records tie each cell and gene therapy vial to one patient. Almost all of this rests on two encryption methods, Rivest-Shamir-Adleman (RSA) and elliptic curve cryptography (ECC). A large enough quantum computer would break both.

'Harvest Now, Decrypt Later' Is Only Half The Problem
Executives who follow quantum risk usually know the 'harvest now, decrypt later' threat. Adversaries steal or intercept encrypted data today and store it until future quantum computers can decrypt it. The theft is getting faster. 

Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 found that the fastest quarter of intrusions reached data exfiltration in 72 minutes in 2025, compared with 285 minutes in 2024. Supply chain data stays valuable for a long time. That includes supplier pricing, bills of materials and patient-linked logistics records. It also includes clinical trial shipment patterns, which show where trials run and how fast they are enrolling. 

A rival who decrypts five-year-old trial supply data in 2032 still learns something useful. But confidentiality is the half of the problem people already know. Integrity is the more dangerous half. Once signatures can be forged, an attacker does not just read your supply chain. They can give it orders.

How Forged Signatures Cause Physical Harm
Forged firmware: Containers and loggers accept signed updates. If the signature can be forged, an attacker can change temperature settings or make devices report 'in range' while the product spoils. That is sabotage at scale, with no broken seal to find.

Forged ownership and release documents: A forged bill of lading or release message can send a high-value shipment to the wrong truck. Cargo theft no longer needs an insider.

Forged partner identities: If an attacker can impersonate a trading partner in the drug tracing system, they can slip counterfeit or diverted products into legitimate channels. For cell therapies, an altered chain-of-identity record is a patient safety disaster, not just a compliance failure.

A fourth problem moves more slowly. Pharmaceutical batch, serialization and chain-of-identity records are kept for years and may be used in lawsuits for decades. Once old-style signatures can be forged, anyone can question whether a record signed that way is authentic.

The Signature Gap
There is a trap here. The industry is adopting quantum-safe encryption faster than quantum-safe signatures. Analysts reviewing the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) January 2026 guidance on post-quantum products pointed to a 'signature gap'. 

Many products support the National Institute of Standards and Technology's (NIST) new standard for exchanging encryption keys (ML-KEM), but support for its signature standard (ML-DSA) is far less common. The result is a 'half-migrated' reality where data in transit is protected against 'harvest now, decrypt later' attacks, but the systems are still vulnerable to future quantum impersonation.

For a bank, that gap is serious. In a supply chain, where signatures control physical equipment, it is the main risk. Replacing signatures means changing the root keys everything else trusts, along with the security hardware that stores them, across dozens of organisations. That is much harder than switching on a new encryption setting.

Why This Is A 2026 Decision
Executives often ask when a quantum computer able to break today's encryption will arrive. Estimates vary. One 2026 analysis says RSA-breaking machines could arrive by 2030, plus or minus three years, and Forrester argues that practical quantum computing by 2030 is likely. For supply chains, though, that is the wrong question.

The better question is how long the equipment you buy this year will stay in service. Refrigerated containers run for over a decade, and industrial controllers often last 20 years or more. A logger shipped today with a fixed RSA key that cannot be updated in the field may still be working when quantum attacks become practical.

Researchers frame this with a simple test called Mosca's inequality. Add two numbers: how long your data must stay secret, or your equipment must stay trustworthy, and how long it will take you to migrate.

If the total is longer than the time until a quantum attack is possible, you are already exposed. In supply chains, equipment lifespan is often what pushes companies over the line. That means purchasing decisions made in 2026 will set quantum exposure in the 2030s.

Policymakers have noticed. In June 2026, the White House issued Executive Order 14409, which warns that "the advent of large-scale quantum computers, particularly in the hands of adversaries, will pose a significant threat to widely used cryptographic security systems." Federal purchasing standards usually spread to private suppliers. Pharma, defence and logistics firms that sell to the government will feel the effect first.

Why The Business Risk Is Easy To Underestimate
From a risk management view, quantum risk has three features that most corporate risk frameworks handle poorly. It hits everyone at once. A broken algorithm does not affect one company. It affects every company that uses it, at the same moment. For cyber insurers, that looks more like a natural catastrophe than a series of separate claims, and the market has struggled to price that kind of system-wide exposure.

It may fall between insurance policies. If forged firmware spoils a shipment, is that a cyber loss, a marine cargo loss or a product recall loss? Each policy may exclude it. The first quantum attackers will probably be nation states, so exclusions for war and state-backed attacks add more uncertainty.

The costs come first and the losses come later. Companies pay to fix the problem now, but the damage arrives years from now, and quarterly incentives favour waiting. Smaller carriers and logistics providers are the weakest links in any multi-company chain, and they have the least money and motivation to upgrade. Their inaction exposes everyone else.

What Leaders Should Do Now
1. Map your cryptography, including your partners'. Build a full inventory of where your company uses encryption and signatures, sometimes called a cryptographic bill of materials. Cover enterprise resource planning (ERP) and warehouse systems, partner connections, IoT devices and controllers, and the hardware that stores your keys. Require key suppliers to provide the same.

2. Rank by impact, not by system. Upgrade first the assets whose compromise would cause physical harm or that will stay in service the longest. Firmware signing for cold-chain devices and remote access to manufacturing usually top the list.

3. Block data harvesting now. Hybrid encryption combines today's methods with quantum-safe ones, and it is already available in mainstream web security and virtual private network (VPN) software. Turn it on for partner data exchanges and vendor maintenance links.

4. Make signatures the priority, and buy flexibility. Every new device contract should require two things: quantum-safe firmware signing and the ability to change keys and algorithms later without replacing hardware, often called crypto agility.

The goal is long-term flexibility rather than performing a one-time upgrade. Small battery-powered loggers may be too limited for large quantum-safe signatures. For those, have the logger use lightweight encryption to talk to a nearby gateway, and let the gateway handle the quantum-safe security.

5. Coordinate with partners and check your insurance. No company can upgrade a supply chain alone. Push for shared timelines through industry bodies such as GS1, the Digital Container Shipping Association and the International Air Transport Association (IATA). Write quantum readiness milestones into supplier contracts, with cost-sharing for smaller partners. Ask your broker directly which policy pays if a forged signature spoils a shipment.

Quantum computing usually reaches the boardroom as an IT upgrade. For any company that makes, moves or stores physical goods, it is really a question of operational resilience. The same cryptography that protects your data also controls your containers, releases your cargo and proves your products are genuine.

The companies that get through the quantum transition well will not be the ones that guessed the date right. They will be the ones that stopped buying equipment that cannot survive it.
